messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

It was a clear, cold morning over the desert when Lieutenant Colonel Marcus Voss’s F-35 suffered a catastrophic engine failure during a routine training sortie. The aircraft pitched violently, and the sudden, deafening roar of a low-altitude explosion filled the cockpit as the turbine disintegrated. Marcus fought the controls for what felt like an eternity before the ejection sequence fired, the force of the blast and the G-forces compressing his spine and sending a searing wave of dizziness through his skull. He landed hard, concussed and disoriented, the smell of burning jet fuel thick in the air. For weeks afterward, the physical effects lingered—a persistent, unshakable lightheadedness that made him feel as though the ground was tilting beneath him, and a queasy, ill sensation that came and went without warning. It was that dizziness, more than any memory of the flames, that became the first crack in his world.

Whenever Marcus felt dizzy or physically unwell, his body would immediately snap into a state of high alert. His muscles would tense, his breath would shorten, and he would find himself scanning the room for an exit, his heart hammering against his ribs as if the explosion was about to happen again. This constant vigilance bled into everything. The unexpected bang of a hangar door closing or a colleague dropping a tool would send a violent jolt through him, his hands flying up defensively. He became convinced that his body was a battlefield, perpetually braced for the next disaster. These same physical sensations also began to corrode his most fundamental beliefs. When the dizziness struck, Marcus would think, *The world is a dangerous place. I am not safe anywhere.* The emotional numbness that followed was the most terrifying part—he felt dead inside, hollowed out, as if the man who had once loved flying had been replaced by a hollow shell. The shattered feeling was not just in his bones; it was in his very understanding of how the world worked.

To manage this, Marcus began to avoid anything medical. He refused his annual flight physical, cancelled a routine check-up for his lingering headaches, and drove past the base hospital with his gaze fixed straight ahead. He reasoned that if he didn't see a doctor, he didn't have to confront the possibility that something was permanently wrong. This avoidance, however, only deepened his sense of being a broken man, reinforcing the idea that he was fundamentally damaged. He also started to strictly control his eating, limiting himself to bland, predictable foods at exact times of day; it was the only domain where he could still exert control, and when he deviated, the resulting indigestion would trigger a full-blown panic, convincing him he was about to pass out. He gave up his weekly poker games with the squadron and stopped taking his wife, Elena, to their favorite restaurant, telling himself he simply didn't have the energy for enjoyment anymore. This self-imposed isolation meant he spent more time alone in the house, where the silence made him hypervigilant to every creak and shadow, and where a sudden movement from Elena in the kitchen would make him flinch so badly she would start to cry.

The cycle tightened over the months. His hypervigilance and constant tension—his body on perpetual alert—drove him deeper into avoidance. He would leave the room if a conversation turned to medical topics, and he began to dread the sound of a motorcycle backfiring or a car door slamming, which would send his heart racing and force him to retreat to the garage to calm down. The more he isolated himself, the more convinced he became that the world was a dangerous place, and the more his emotional numbness grew. He started to feel that he had become a stranger to himself, a ghost haunting his own home. What finally brought him to the clinic was a morning when a minor dizzy spell in the shower spiraled into a full panic attack. He stood there, dripping wet, certain he was going to die, and he realized he could no longer pretend this was just a phase. He came to the appointment not because he believed he could be fixed, but because he was terrified that if he didn't, he would lose Elena, his career, and the last shred of himself that he still recognized.
